segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life . I'm Ira Glass. OK, so for months around here at our radio show, we have all been preparing for this day today. The date of this day has been written on our white board in big letters for months, because this is the day that we launch our first real spin-off. As of today, we're not making just one weekly show here, but two shows.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Our second show is called Serial . That's not like breakfast, but the kind of serial where one thing follows another. And I've mentioned this show on the air before. But just in case you missed that, here's the premise of the new show. Instead of each episode bringing you a different theme and different stories, every episode of Serial brings you back to the exact same story and tells you the next chapter in that story.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is a long story told over a dozen episodes, a true story. One of our producers and regular contributors, Sarah Koenig, is going to be hosting the new series. And the first story Serial is taking on is about a murder.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's a case where what really happened is actually much more complicated than the jury ever heard when this thing went to trial. And each week we will go with Sarah on her hunt to figure out what really happened. And we will learn the answers as she does.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Our new show, by the way, is not a radio show. It's a podcast. I'll explain more about that later in the hour. And what we're going to do today here on the radio is play you the first episode. OK, and so with that, here's Sarah. And I really hope you like this.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: For the last year, I've spent every working day trying to figure out where a high school kid was for an hour after school one day in 1999-- or if you want to get technical about it, and apparently I do, where a high school kid was for 21 minutes after school one day in 1999. This search sometimes feels undignified on my part. I've had to ask about teenagers' sex lives, where, how often, with whom, about notes they passed in class, about their drug habits, their relationships with their parents.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And I'm not a detective or a private investigator. I've not even a crime reporter. But, yes, every day this year, I've tried to figure out the alibi of a 17-year-old boy. Before I get into why I've been doing this, I just want to point out something I'd never really thought about before I started working on this story. And that is, it's really hard to account for your time, in a detailed way, I mean.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: How'd you get to work last Wednesday, for instance? Drive? Walk? Bike? Was it raining? Are you sure?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Did you go to any stores that day? If so, what did you buy? Who did you talk to? The entire day, name every person you talked to. It's hard.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Now imagine you have to account for a day that happened six weeks back. Because that's the situation in the story I'm working on in which a bunch of teenagers had to recall a day six weeks earlier. And it was 1999, so they had to do it without the benefit of texts or Facebook or Instagram. Just for a lark, I asked some teenagers to try it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Do you remember what you did on that Friday?

segments.speaker: Tyler
segments.text: No. Not at all. I can't remember anything.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Wait, nothing?

segments.speaker: Tyler
segments.text: No. I can't remember anything that far back. I'm pretty sure I was in school. I think-- no?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: That's Tyler. He's 18. I asked my nephew Sam. He's 18, too.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Not a clue. In school, probably. I would be in school. Actually, I think I worked that day. Yeah, I worked that day. And I went to school. That was about it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Actually, on second thought?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: I don't think I went to school that day.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: You don't think you went.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah, no, I didn't. I definitely didn't.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Here's Sam's friend Elliot. He seemed to have better recall.

segments.speaker: Elliot
segments.text: Actually, I may have gone to the movies that night later.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Do you remember what you saw?

segments.speaker: Elliot
segments.text: Now that I'm thinking. I'm sorry? Yeah, I think I saw 22 Jump Street .

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: OK. And did you go with friends?

segments.speaker: Elliot
segments.text: Yeah. I went with Sam and this kid Sean, Carter, a bunch of people.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Wait, Sam, my nephew Sam?

segments.speaker: Elliot
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, OK. So Sam says he was at work.

segments.speaker: Elliot
segments.text: Oh, then it wasn't that night, then.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: One kid did actually remember pretty well, because it was the last day of state testing at his school and he'd saved up to go to a nightclub. That's the main thing I learned from this exercise, which is no big shocker, I guess. If some significant event happened that day, you remember that, plus you remember the entire day much better.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: If nothing significant happened, then the answers get very general. I most likely did this, or I most likely did that. These are words I've heard a lot lately. Here's the case I've been working on.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Almost 15 years ago, on January 13, 1999, a girl named Hae Min Lee disappeared. She was a senior at Woodlawn High School in Baltimore County in Maryland. She was Korean. She was smart, and beautiful, and cheerful, and a great athlete. She played field hockey and lacrosse. And she was responsible.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Right after school she was supposed to pick up her little cousin from kindergarten and drop her home. But she didn't show. That's when Hae Lee's family knew something was up, when the cousin's school called.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: About a month later, on February 9, Hae's body was found in a big park in Baltimore, really a rambling forest. A maintenance guy who said he'd stopped to take a leak on his way to work discovered her there. He'd noticed a bit of her black hair poking out of a shallow grave.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: The cause of death was manual strangulation, meaning someone did it with their hands. A couple weeks after that, so six weeks after she first went missing, Hae's ex-boyfriend, a guy named Adnan Syed, was arrested for her murder. He's been in prison ever since.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I first heard about this story more than a year ago when I got an email from a woman named Rabia Chaudry. Rabia knows Adnan pretty well. Her younger brother Saad is Adnan's best friend. And they believe he's innocent.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Rabia was writing to me because, way back when, I used to be a reporter for the Baltimore Sun , and she'd come across some stories I'd written about a well-known defense attorney in Baltimore who'd been disbarred for mishandling client money. That attorney was the same person who defended Adnan, her last major trial, in fact.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Rabia told me she thought the attorney botched the case-- not just botched it, actually, but threw the case on purpose so she could get more money for the appeal. The lawyer had died a few years later. She'd been sick.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Rabia asked if I would please just take a look at Adnan's case. I don't get emails like this every day. So I thought, sure, why not?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I read a few newspaper clips about the case, looked up a few trial records. And on paper, the case was like a Shakespearean mashup-- young lovers from different worlds thwarting their families, secret assignations, jealousy, suspicion, and honor besmirched, the villain not a Moor exactly, but a Muslim all the same, and a final act of murderous revenge. And the main stage? A regular old high school across the street from a 7-Eleven.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Hi, are you Rabia? Hi. Am I saying your name correctly?

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: Rabia.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Rabia. OK.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I went to go see Rabia. She was surrounded by paper-- files, loose stacks, binders, some crappy looking boxes-- all court documents and attorney's files from Adnan's case. Some of the papers were warped and discolored.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Why do they look wet? They look wet.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: These have been damaged, because these--

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: She explained that it was because the boxes had been in her car, on and off, for 15 years. Rabia is a lawyer herself. She mostly does immigration stuff. Her office takes up the corner of a much larger open space that I think is a Pakistani travel agency, though it's hard to tell.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: It's in this little strip mall. Across the parking lot, there's a new Pakistani restaurant, an African evangelical church, an Indian clothing shop, a convenience store. On the sidewalk outside, I found a teeny weeny bag of marijuana.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Baltimore County is like this, at least on the west side. It's where a lot of middle class and working class people go, many immigrants included, to get their kids out of the badass city. Though the badass city is close by.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Rabia is 40. She's short, and she's got a beautiful round face framed by hijab. She's adorable looking, but you definitely shouldn't mess with her. She's very smart and very tough, and she could crush you.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Her brother Saad was at Rabia's office too the first time I went. He's 33, a mortgage broker, more laid back than Rabia. They told me about Adnan Syed, their friend-- not just a good kid, but an especially good kid-- smart, kind, goofy, handsome. So that when he was arrested for murder, so many people who know him were stunned.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: He was like the community's golden child.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, really? Talk more about that.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: He was an honor roll student, volunteer EMT. He was on the football team. He was a star runner on the track team. He was the homecoming king. He led prayers at the mosque. Everybody knew Adnan to be somebody who was going to do something really big.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I later fact checked all these accolades, of course, and learned that Rabia was mostly right, though she sometimes gets a little loosey-goosey with the details. Adnan was an EMT, but he didn't volunteer. He was paid for it. He was on the track team, but he wasn't a star. He did play football. And he did lead prayers on occasion.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: He wasn't homecoming king. But he was prince of his junior prom, and this at a high school that was majority black. They picked the Pakistani Muslim kid. So you get the picture. He was an incredibly likable and well-liked kid.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: This conversation with Rabia and Saad, this is what launched me on this yearlong-- "obsession" is maybe too strong a word-- let's say fascination with this case. By the end of this hour, you're going to hear different people tell different versions of what happened the day Hae Lee was killed. But let's start with the most important version of the story, the one Rabia told me first. And that's the one that was presented at trial.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: The state's case against Adnan went like this. He and Hae had been going out since junior prom. But Adnan wasn't supposed to be dating at all. Adnan was born in the US, but his parents are from Pakistan. And they're conservative Muslims-- no drinking, no smoking, no girls, all that.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Saad and Rabia's parents are the same way. Their families are friends. But even though Adnan and Saad and their buddies were Muslims, they were also, shall we say, healthy American teenagers who were going to do what teenagers do, so long as they didn't get caught.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So Adnan had to keep his relationship with Hae secret. The state used this against him in two ways. First, they argued, he put everything on the line-- his family, his relationships at the mosque-- to run around with this girl. So that when she broke up with him eight months later, he was left with nothing, and he was outraged. He couldn't take it, and he killed her.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And the second way they used it, as they said-- look at what a liar he is, how duplicitous. He plays the good Muslim son at home and at the mosque, but look what he was up to. Saad remembers the prosecutor's closing argument at trial.

segments.speaker: Saad
segments.text: His family didn't know that he actually drank, he smoked, he was having sex.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: This was proof of bad character, someone who could be a murderer. But Saad says, if Adnan is guilty of anything, it's of being a normal kid with immigrant parents.

segments.speaker: Saad
segments.text: So the prosecution had painted Adnan as a totally bipolar or a maniacal dual personality.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: We all grew up with that dual personality.

segments.speaker: Saad
segments.text: I know, it was forced. I'm the same way. I was like, they could paint the same thing. Because I was actually homecoming king, which I don't know if my sister even knows.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: I did not know this.

segments.speaker: Saad
segments.text: She did not know. So I was dating a girl that was--

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And why is homecoming king bad? That sounds like a good thing.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: We don't go to homecoming. We don't--

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Because it's a dance.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: It's a dance. It's a mixed gender--

segments.speaker: Saad
segments.text: So I was in the same boat. My parents, my sister, they didn't know about this at all. Right now, more than 10 year later, she's finding out. I know, I'll admit. On one side, my family thinks I'm a virgin. But on the other hand, I play-- you know.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: --way too much.

segments.speaker: Saad
segments.text: But it's the truth.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: TMI, TMI, TMI.

segments.speaker: Saad
segments.text: See that? That right there is kind of making her feel uncomfortable. She's like, whoa, whoa, whoa.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So just on motive alone, Saad and Rabia found the whole thing ridiculous. As for physical evidence, there was none-- nothing. Apart from some fingerprints in Hae's car, which Adnan had been in many times, there was nothing linking him to the crime-- no DNA, no fibers, no hairs, no matching soil from the bottom of his boots.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Instead, what they had on Adnan was one guy's story, a guy named Jay. He's the third person you need to remember in this crime story besides Hae and Adnan. Jay was a friend of Adnan's. They'd been in school together since middle school.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: They weren't super close, but they had mutual friends. Jay sold weed, and he and Adnan smoked together. The story Jay told police had problems, because it kept changing from telling to telling. But they were able to bolster the main plot points using cell records from Adnan's phone.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: By the time I left Rabia's office that first day, I understood only one thing clearly, though maybe not the thing Rabia and Saad wanted me to understand. But what I took away from the visit was, somebody is lying here. Maybe Adnan really is innocent. But what if he isn't? What if he did do it, and he's got all these good people thinking he didn't?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So either it's Jay or it's Adnan. But someone is lying. And I really wanted to figure out who.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: In the early morning of February 28, 1999, Adnan was arrested by Baltimore City detectives. He was asleep in his bed when they showed up at his house. They took him straight from his untidy bedroom to an interrogation room at Homicide downtown. What Adnan didn't know is that just hours before they picked him up, the cops had interviewed his friend Jay.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: This is a taped interview of Jay, black male, 19 years of age. We're at the offices of Homicide, specifically the colonel's conference room.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: The police recorded two taped interviews with Jay. And I'm going to play you the second one from a couple weeks later, only because the sound quality is much better. Just a warning that the tape is a little upsetting to hear in parts.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Why don't you go ahead and tell us what you know about the death of Hae Lee.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: OK. I'd left out, went shopping with a friend of mine, an ex-friend of mine, Adnan. We had had a conversation. During the conversation he stated that he was going to kill that bitch, referring to Hae Lee. I took it with context. It didn't stand out in my head any.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Jay said he didn't take it too seriously. The cops have him start again from the top. On the morning of the 13th, Jay says, Adnan had left school and driven to Jay's house. Jay had graduated from school the year before and was working, but not on that day.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: January 13 happens to be the birthday of Jay's girlfriend, Stephanie. And Jay, who didn't have his own car, needed to go buy something for her. So Adnan comes over. According to Jay, they go shopping at the mall.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: When did you do that?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: We left the mall. I took him to school. I dropped him off in the back of the school. He went up to class. He left his cell phone in the car with me, told me he'd call me. I went back to my friend James' house and waited for him to call.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: OK, now at this point, you know why he's leaving the car with you.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: And why is that?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Because he said he was going to kill Hae.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: And the reason you have the car and the cell phone was why?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: To pick him up from wherever he was going to do this at.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: OK, and you had talked about this while you were shopping that day?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: The details of the car and all?

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: The events, how they were going to plan out.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: That day he told me, yes. He told me, I'm going to leave you with my cellphone and my car, and I need you to come get me. Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: After--

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: After he had killed Hae, yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Later that afternoon, the call comes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: You received a phone call from Adnan.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: On his cellphone.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Which is in your possession.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: And the conversation was what?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: That bitch is dead. Come and get me. I'm at Best Buy.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Jay drives to Best Buy and sees Adnan in the parking lot.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: I noticed that Hae wasn't with him. I parked next to him. He asked me to get out the car. I get out the car. He asks me, am I ready for this? And I say, ready for what?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: And he takes the keys. He opens the trunk. And all I can see is Hae's lips are all blue, and she's pretzeled up in the back of the trunk. And she's dead.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: They leave the parking lot. Adnan's driving Hae's car with her body in the trunk. Jay's driving Adnan's car. They ditch Hae's car at the I-70 park and ride. And then, to hear Jay tell it, they just kind of tool around Baltimore County together for a while as if nothing had happened-- buy some weed, cruise around, make some calls. After a while, Jay drives Adnan back to Woodlawn High School.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Why did you take him back to school?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: He told me that I had to take him back to school because he needed to be seen there.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Was he going to a certain event?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: It was practice, track practice.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Track practice.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: So he wanted an alibi?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: He wanted to be seen by people at track.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: And you guys had discussed that?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: He just told me that he needed to be seen.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: He told me that he needed to be seen.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: At track practice. You took him back?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Are you having any conversation with Adnan at the time?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: To the effect, yes. Don't tell anyone. He said that he couldn't believe he killed somebody with his bare hands, that all the other mother [BLEEP] referring to hoods and thugs and stuff think they're hard core. But he just killed a person with his bare hands.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: So at this point he's bragging about it?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Basically.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: He was proud of it?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: After track practice, Jay picks Adnan up again. They drive around some more. By this time, Hae's family was worried, and they'd called the police, who in turn called a couple of Hae's friends, including Adnan.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: The call comes in on his cell. The cops ask if he's seen Hae or knows where she is. Jay says after the call, they drive to Jay's to get some shovels, go retrieve Hae's car from the park and ride. They drive around some more and finally end up at Lincoln Park, where Adnan proceeds to bury Hae. It's evening by now, maybe 7:00 or 8:00 PM.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: And he asked me if I was going to help. And I told him, [BLEEP] no. And he starts just shoveling dirt on top of her. After we leave there--

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Let me stop there.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: You helped him dig the hole.

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: How long did it take you both to dig the hole?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: 20, 25 minutes.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: How deep did you make the hole?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Oh, maybe six inches at the most. It wasn't very deep at all.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Who did most of the digging?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Uh, it was--

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Both of you?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: Equal work?

segments.speaker: Jay
segments.text: I wouldn't say that, but yeah.

segments.speaker: Detective
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So those are the key points. Adnan told Jay in advance he was going to do it. He did it. They buried her. Jay's story wasn't just the foundation of the state's case against Adnan. It was the state's case against Adnan.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: In the picture Jay drew, it's cold. I mean, he's not describing a crime of passion here. This is something much darker-- to methodically map out the death of your friend, to strangle her with your own hands so close up like that. That would mean Adnan wasn't just a killer, but a master liar and manipulator, a psychopath, probably.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Adnan's in a maximum security prison in western Maryland. He calls me at my request about twice a week. He talks to me from a bank of eight pay phones in the rec hall, a pretty large room where other guys are sitting at tables with metal seats attached to them playing chess or cards or using the microwave or watching TV.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: It can get a little loud sometimes. Once I asked if all eight phones were always occupied. And he said, usually not, because guys who have been in for a long time, often they have no one to call.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: When I first met Adnan in person, I was struck by two things. He was way bigger than I expected-- barrel chested and tall. In the photos I'd seen, he was still a lanky teenager with struggling facial hair and sagging jeans. By now, he was 32. He'd spent nearly half his life in prison, becoming larger and properly bearded.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And the second thing, which you can't miss about Adnan, is that he has giant brown eyes like a dairy cow. That's what prompts my most idiotic lines of inquiry. Could someone who looks like that really strangle his girlfriend? Idiotic, I know.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: When he first heard Jay's story of the crime, Adnan didn't say, well, it didn't happen like that, or, I didn't mean for it to happen like that. He said, it didn't happen. None of this is true at all. He says he had nothing to do with Hae's murder, and he doesn't know who did.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Hae was Adnan's first serious relationship with a girl. He says he loved her in the way of high school love, but then also in the way of high school got over her. So that when they broke up for good sometime before Christmas break of senior year, he says he was sad for sure, but not obsessed or anything.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: I just sometimes wish they could look into my brain and see how I really felt about her. And no matter what else someone would say, they would see, man, this guy had no ill will toward her. Whatever the motivation is to kill someone, I had absolutely-- it didn't exist in me, you know what I mean? No one can ever say why.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: People could say why. Oh, man, he was mad, this, that, or the other. But no one could ever come with any type of proof or anecdote or anything to ever say that I was ever mad at her, that I was ever angry with her, that I ever threatened her. That's the only thing I can really hold onto. That is like my only firm handhold in this whole thing, that no one's ever been able to prove it.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: No one ever has been able to provide any shred of evidence that I had anything but friendship toward her, like love and respect for her. That's at the end of the day, man. The only thing I can ever say is, man, I had no reason to kill her.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: He's adamant about this. You can hear it, right? He's staunch. The problem is, when you ask Adnan to go back and tell his version of what happened that day, to refute Jay's story, everything becomes a lot mushier.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Yes, he hung out with Jay on the 13th, both during and after school. But he doesn't remember exactly where they went, or what they did, or what time it was. Here's what he's got.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: January 13 unfolded like any other day, a normal, mostly uneventful day. He says there are a couple of things that do stand out, though. That day was Stephanie's birthday. Stephanie was one of Adnan's best friends and also Jay's girlfriend.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Adnan had gotten Stephanie a birthday present, a stuffed reindeer, which he'd given to her in second period, Miss Ephron's English class.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: And it occurred to me that day that I was going to ask her boyfriend, Jay, did he get her a gift? So sometime during the day before noon--

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Wait, Adnan, just hold up for a second. Why did you care whether Jay got Stephanie a present? What's it to you?

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: Well, Stephanie was a very close friend of mine, as I mentioned. And I just kind of wanted to make sure that she also got a gift from him, you know? She had mentioned to me that she was looking forward to getting a gift from him. She mentioned that she was really happy to get the gift that I gave her.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: So as I would with any friend, I just kind of went to check on that. I kind of had a feeling that maybe he didn't get her a gift. And I had free periods during school. So it was not abnormal for me to leave school to go do something and then come back.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: So I went to his house. And I asked him, did you happen to get a present for Stephanie? He said no. So I said, if you want to, you can drop me back off to school. You can borrow my car. And you can go to the mall and get her a gift or whatever. Then just come pick me up after track practice that day.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So then what happened?

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: Well, then when school was over, I would have went to the library. I know that I usually check-- well, I didn't usually check. But if I was going to check my email, it would be using the library computer. You know, sometimes I would go there because track practice didn't start until around maybe 3 o'clock or 3:30-ish.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: So it didn't start right after school. So there was a period of time of almost like an hour, an hour and some change, that was kind of free time.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: This hour and change after school, this is the crucial window. This is the time when the state says Hae was killed. School got out at 2:15. People remember seeing her after her last class heading to her car.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: According to Jay's story and the cellphone records, she was dead by 2:36 PM. So sometime in those 21 minutes, between 2:15 and 2:36, she was strangled. So that's obviously the same window Adnan needed to account for. To quote Adnan, "My case lived and died in those 21 minutes."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So where does Adnan say he was? Well, maybe the library, but nobody testified to that at trial. Then to track practice-- he does remember being at track one day when it was snowing, which might have been that day. The coach testified that Adnan probably was there, but he can't be 100% sure because, as a rule, he didn't take attendance. After school is when his memories become nonspecific. Usually we did this, or we probably would have done that.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: Probably track practice would have ended  like, I'd say, 4:30.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Jay did come to pick up Adnan after track. That part Adnan seems to more or less remember. It was Ramadan, so Adnan would have been fasting all day and hungry.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: It probably would've been close to time for me to break fast. He would have came to pick me up, and we would have went to go get something to eat. And then we would have smoked some weed after, right? And then I would have had to have been home around 7, 8 o'clock, right?

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: Or usually like the last 10 nights of Ramadan, my father would spend the night at the mosque. So a lot of times I would take him food. I think my mother would make food for him, and I would take it usually before 8 o'clock. Because that's the last evening prayer.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Did you ever leave the campus before the end of track practice? Did you ever--

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: You're sure?

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: I want to say that I'm 99% sure.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: The reason why I can't say 100 is because-- I mean, I do kind of understand that it comes across as-- I don't know if it does or doesn't. But it seems like I remember things that are beneficial to me, but things that aren't beneficial to me I can't remember. It's just that I don't really know what to say beyond the fact that a lot of the day that I do remember, it's bits and pieces that comes from what other people have said that they remember, right? And it kind of jogs my memory.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: Yeah. I don't really know what to say. And I completely understand how that comes across. I mean, the only thing I can say is, man, it was just a normal day to me. There was absolutely nothing abnormal about that day.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Adnan knows better than anyone how unhelpful this all is, how problematic. Because it plays both ways. If he's innocent, right, it's any other day. Of course he doesn't remember.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But you can also read it as, how convenient. He doesn't remember the day. So no one can fact check him, or poke holes in his story. Because he has no story.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: I definitely understand that someone could look at this and say, oh, man, he must be lying. It's so coincidental that he doesn't remember what he did this particular time. I mean, I completely understand that, and I get that. Like I said, that's the hardest thing I've dealt with for these past 15 years.

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: There's nothing tangible I can do to remember that day. There's nothing I can do to make me remember. I've pored through the transcripts. I've looked through the telephone records. What else can I do?

segments.speaker: Adnan
segments.text: There's nothing I can do. So perhaps I'll never be able to explain it. And it is what it is. If someone believes me or not, you know, I have no control over it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Adnan's trial was a long ordeal. Jay was on the stand for something like five days. A cellphone expert testified for two days, a lifetime when you're discussing cell tower technology. There were absences, and some bad weather closed the courts. So it was six weeks before both sides rested.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But the jury? They moved like lightning. After just a few hours, including a lunch break, they convicted Adnan of first-degree murder. Rabia Chaudry was there in the courtroom when it happened. She says his mother was crying. She was crying.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Rabia hadn't sat through the whole trial. So the first time she fully understood that the case came down to those 21 minutes was during closing arguments, when the prosecutor brought out a dummy's head and strangled it in front of the jury. That evening, after the verdict, Rabia went to see Adnan in lockup.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: And so I went to go see him. So this is the same day he's been convicted. And this is the first time I actually had a conversation with him about, what's going on? And I was like, you know, Adnan, the whole thing's turning on these 20, 25 minutes. Where were you?

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: And he's like, she disappeared in January, you know? In March, you're asking me, where were you after school for 20 minutes on a specific day? All the days are the same to me, you know?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But then he mentions that there was this one girl, an alibi girl.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: He's like, the only thing I could offer is I remember there's a girl I go to school with. Her name's Asia McLean. He's like, right after I got arrested, she wrote me a couple of letters. And she said she also went to see my family. And she said she specifically remembers me being at the library, at the public library, right after school.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: The Woodlawn public library is just across the parking lot from Woodlawn High School. It's not technically part of the campus, but it might as well be.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: He said, I gave those letters to Christina Gutierrez, to my attorney. He's like, but apparently it didn't really check out. So he's like, I don't know. So they're not helpful to us. So this was the first time I heard of this girl Asia McLean. I had never heard of her before. Nobody had mentioned her before.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Were you floored, like, wait, wait, wait, wait, what? I mean, like--

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: I wasn't floored at the time. Because I thought, if this girl wrote and the attorney-- what criminal defense attorney's not going to check out a potential alibi? So I asked him, I said, do you have a copy of those letters? He said, yeah, I have a copy. I said, send me a copy.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Adnan sends the letters to Rabia, and here's what she reads. The first letter, the first of two, is dated March 1, 1999. That is one day after Adnan was arrested. At the top of the letter, she notes, "I just came from your house an hour ago.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Dear Adnan-- I hope I spelled it right. I'm not sure if you remember talking to me in the library on January 13, but I remember chatting with you." She says, quote, "we aren't really close friends, but I want you to look into my eyes and tell me of your innocence. If I ever find otherwise, I will hunt you down and whip your ass. OK, friend?" At the bottom she added a little note. "My boyfriend and his best friend remember seeing you there, too."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: That's letter number one. Then the next day, on March 2, she writes Adnan another letter. This one's typed. It's chattier. She talks about the gossip at school, the bits and pieces of evidence about the crime that are circulating, what the students are saying, what the teachers are saying, about her visit to his house.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Quote, "Your brothers are nice. I don't think I met your mother. I think I met your dad. Does he have a big gray beard? They gave me and Justin soda and cake. There was a whole bunch of people at your house. I didn't know who they were.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I also didn't know that Muslims take their shoes off in the house. Thank God they didn't make me take mine off. My stinky feet probably would have knocked everyone out cold. Why haven't you told anyone about talking to me in the library?" she asks him. "Did you think it was unimportant? You didn't think that I would remember? Or did you just totally forget yourself?"

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Adnan says now that he does in fact remember seeing Asia in the library. The thing he remembers about it is so high school. Asia used to go out with Adnan's friend Justin. And Justin had confided that Asia was a proper young lady." In other words, Justin wasn't getting any.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So Adnan remembers thinking he would now get to tease Justin about seeing Asia with her new boyfriend. Maybe the new guy was getting lucky, ha, ha. Anyway, Rabia calls Asia up. It's been a year since she wrote the letters, but she agrees to meet.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: And she told me, that day after school I went to the public library. And Adnan was sitting at a computer, checking email or something. And I sat down next to him. We started chatting. And Adnan was a very popular boy in school. He was handsome and popular with the ladies.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: So she was speaking to him. And her boyfriend shows up a little bit later with a friend. And she said her boyfriend was really angry at her, because he's like, why are you talking to him? You know, high school kids, why are you talking to him? Is he hitting on you?

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: And she remembered very specifically that that day she went to her boyfriend's house with him, and they got snowed in. And it snowed really heavily that night. And she remembered that for the following two days, school was closed. So she had very specific details about why she remembered that day.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Asia wrote out an affidavit on the spot. In it, she says she and Adnan spoke for about 15 to 20 minutes while she was waiting for her boyfriend to give her a ride. Quote, "We left around 2:40," unquote. Remember, Hae is supposed to be dead by 2:36. And then, the kicker-- "No attorney has ever contacted me about January 13, 1999 and the above information."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So benefit of the doubt for a second-- maybe Adnan never actually showed the letters to Christina Gutierrez, his attorney. Sure, he said he did, but who knows? Well, I know. Deep inside Gutierrez's notes on the case-- I have boxes and boxes of such stuff-- there's this in her handwriting. "Asia plus boyfriend saw him in library 2:15 to 3:15."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Then there's another note, dated July 13. It's more than four months after Adnan's arrest. This is written by one of Gutierrez's law clerks, who visited Adnan in jail. Quote, "Asia McLean saw him in the library at 3:00. Asia boyfriend saw him too. Library may have cameras."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Why, oh, why was this person never heard from at trial-- a solid, non-crazy, detail-oriented alibi witness in a case that so sorely needed alibi witnesses? I can't ask Christina Gutierrez, because she died in 2004.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So I put that question to a few defense attorneys. And they said, well, alibi witnesses can be tricky, especially if it's just one person. Because then it becomes one person's word over another. A single witness like that can backfire under cross-examination. Or they might take the jury's focus away from the weaknesses in the state's case.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So there are conceivable strategic reasons why Christina Gutierrez might not have wanted to put Asia McLean on the stand. But what is inconceivable, they all said, is to not ever contact Asia McLean, to never make the call, never check it out, never find out if her story helps or hurts your case. That makes no sense whatsoever. That is not a strategy. That is a screw-up.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: When I first heard about the long-lost Asia letters and the lawyer's mistake, I thought, well, their fight is over, right? They've got an alibi witness who was never heard from. It's such a slam dunk. They're done.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Adnan's family hired a new attorney, who filed a petition in court based on the Asia affidavit. His argument was that Adnan's trial could have turned out differently if Gutierrez had checked out Asia's story. And so Adnan should get some form of what's called post-conviction relief.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: The new lawyer figures he'll get Asia to come to the hearing. She'll vouch for her story. By this time, Asia had finished school and moved away. He finds an address on the West Coast, tries calling, sending messages-- nothing. Finally, he writes a letter to her, gives it to a private investigator, who goes out to Asia's house in hopes of delivering it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Asia's fiance comes to the door, opens it part way, tells the investigator that she cannot speak to Asia, but that from what he knows of Adnan's case, Adnan is guilty and deserved the punishment he got. Later, the investigator gets a call from the fiance. "We don't have to talk to you. Leave us alone."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So Adnan's lawyer calls off the search for Asia, figuring once a witness turns on you like that, it's too risky to keep pushing. And then at Adnan's hearing on the new petition, it comes out that Asia had done the very thing they dreaded. Asia had called one of the prosecutors in Adnan's case, a guy named Kevin Urick, and undermined her own statement. This is from a recording of the hearing. Mr. Urick is testifying on the witness stand.

segments.speaker: Attorney
segments.text: Mr. Urick, how did you learn that the [INAUDIBLE] petition?

segments.speaker: Kevin Urick
segments.text: A young lady named Asia called me.

segments.speaker: Attorney
segments.text: And what did she say?

segments.speaker: Kevin Urick
segments.text: She was concerned, because she was being asked questions about an affidavit she'd written back at the time of the trial. She told me that she'd only written it because she was getting pressure from the family, and she basically wrote it to please them and get them off her back.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: I don't know what happened to her and why she would do this.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Here's Rabia again. She says it's not true that Asia was bullied into writing that statement 15 years ago. And she can't fathom why Asia would discredit her own statement like that.

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: I don't know why. The affidavit was written voluntarily. I'm an attorney. I'm a licensed attorney. I work on homeland security. I have no reason to make something like this up. I didn't even know she existed until after the conviction.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So what do you think happened? Why would they have this sort of violent reaction to helping out Adnan now?

segments.speaker: Rabia
segments.text: I don't know. It was just really odd.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So who knows what would have happened if Asia had shown up? Maybe it wouldn't have made a difference. After all, they had the original letters and the affidavit. That's all that should've mattered. But it didn't look good.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: It would be natural for the judge to wonder, why can't the defense produce this Asia person? Why is she making this call to a prosecutor? I mean, anyone would wonder. I wondered. I wondered if maybe she was pressured into writing that affidavit. And I wondered if she was hiding something.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Like maybe she'd lied in those 1999 letters. Maybe she didn't really see Adnan at the library that day and had just wanted to insert herself into something exciting. And maybe now that she was grown up, she wanted nothing to do with any of it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So three, four months after I first sat down with Rabia, I had become fixated on finding Asia. I'm like a bloodhound on this thing. Because the whole case seemed to me to be teetering on her memories of that afternoon. I have to know if Adnan really was in the library at 2:36 PM.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Because if he was, library equals innocent. It's so maddeningly simple. And maybe I can crack it if I could just talk to Asia.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I write her a long, gentle, pleading letter and send it off to an address I find online. I'm calling people who know her or  who I think might know her. I'm checking the same loop of Facebook, MyLife, LinkedIn sites over and over, trawling for clues about where she might be or how she might think.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: If you're wondering why I went so nuts on this story versus some other murder case, the best I can explain is this is the one that came to me. It wasn't halfway across the world or even next door. It came right to my lap. And if I could help get to the bottom of it, shouldn't I try?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I start running down all the other information in Asia's 1999 letters. She mentioned there were security cameras inside the library. So my producer and I went to see the very nice manager there, Michelle Hamiel.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Was there a security system back in '99 that could've been checked at the time?

segments.speaker: Michelle Hamiel
segments.text: Probably, yes. I'm going to say yes.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: OK. And what system was it?

segments.speaker: Michelle Hamiel
segments.text: I have no idea. [LAUGHING] It was an old system.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Yeah. But you think probably video?

segments.speaker: Michelle Hamiel
segments.text: It was video. And that was part of set up. Every morning you put a videotape in.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Were you guys recycling the videotapes?

segments.speaker: Michelle Hamiel
segments.text: Yes. I think it ran for a week. So you had a Monday tape, a Tuesday tape, a Wednesday tape, and so forth.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So even if, on the very day that Asia had written her first letter, Adnan's lawyer had run out to find the security tape, it probably would have been nonexistent by then. But what about the computer Adnan was supposedly using to check his email?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: To use the computer, did people have to sign in, write their name down?

segments.speaker: Michelle Hamiel
segments.text: They did.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And what was the system then?

segments.speaker: Michelle Hamiel
segments.text: Piece of paper and pencil.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And those, by any chance, weren't logged meticulously and kept for 15 years, were they?

segments.speaker: Michelle Hamiel
segments.text: No. [LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Bummer. We got nothing.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Then there was the mystery of Asia's boyfriend, Derek, and his friend Jerrod. All winter and spring, every time I went to Baltimore, I went to Derek's mom's house looking for him, and to Jerrod's window tinting business. And then finally--

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: All right, so you're Jerrod Johnson.

segments.speaker: Jerrod Johnson
segments.text: Yes, I am.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: You don't know how excited we are to be talking to you. I've been looking for you for, like, four months.

segments.speaker: Jerrod Johnson
segments.text: What did I do?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: You didn't do anything. But we were hoping maybe you remembered this moment. On January 13, 1999, do you have any memory, by any miracle, that you went to Woodlawn public library branch near Woodlawn High School to pick up Asia McLean with your friend Derek?

segments.speaker: Jerrod Johnson
segments.text: I have no idea. Asia McLean. Is that a person or a book?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: It's a person.

segments.speaker: Jerrod Johnson
segments.text: No, no recollection of it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Scratch Jerrod. Derek was my last hope. Eventually I caught him at home. Considering I woke him up, he was exceedingly courteous. He showed me a photo of Asia and him all dressed up. They dated most of senior year.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: What's up here?

segments.speaker: Derek
segments.text: This is our senior prom. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: You guys both look really beautiful.

segments.speaker: Derek
segments.text: Yeah. That's Asia, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But Derek couldn't remember that day either-- shocking, I know. He used to pick Asia up from school almost every day back then, either from the library or from the front of the school. And he says he spoke to a lot of her friends just to be polite.

segments.speaker: Derek
segments.text: And it's very possible that I could have spoken to the gentleman and her on that day. But it's very hard to remember 15 years later. But it sounds like this definitely could have happened. I don't think Asia would-- Asia's not the type of person that would lie just to--

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: That's what I'm wondering.

segments.speaker: Derek
segments.text: She's definitely not that type of person to get involved with a lie. She's not that type of person. So it seemed pretty credible to me.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: One day I get a call on my cellphone from a blocked number.

segments.speaker: Asia Mclean
segments.text: I mean, I have a couple minutes if you want to chat about it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: You guessed it-- Asia.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, what Asia remembers, which is a lot. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues. It's This American Life . I'm Ira Glass. Today on our program, Sarah Koenig looks into the murder of a Baltimore teenager back in 1999. Our story continues. You remember where we left off. Sarah had been looking for Asia McLean. Here's Sarah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I wish I could say that my charming, persuasive letter is what prompted Asia to call. But the truth is, she never got my letter. I had the wrong address. But she was calling because I'd followed up weeks later with a one-line email. And she was responding to that, a little confused.

segments.speaker: Asia Mclean
segments.text: It's just crazy. I mean, I have a couple minutes if you want to chat about it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I recorded our conversation on the cell, which is why the sound quality is so bad. Sorry about that. Asia is now a 33-year-old stay-at-home mother. And she has not spent the last 15 years worrying about Adnan and whether he's guilty.

segments.speaker: Asia Mclean
segments.text: I trust the court system to do their due diligence. Because I was never questioned. I was never informed of anything pertaining to the case. I don't know why he was convicted.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Asia said she was spooked when the private investigator came to her house. I don't know if that's why she didn't testify at the hearing or why she made the call to the prosecutor. But she told me that when she got the knock at the door, quote, "that was not cool." Because to her, if Adnan did do it, quote, "the last thing you want is a murderer being pissed off at you, knowing where you live."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But she had a remarkably clear memory of what happened on January 13, 1999. She had an internship at the time, and so she got out of school much earlier than everyone else. Derek was supposed to come get her at the library along with Jerrod, but they were very late. She remembers seeing Adnan come in after Woodlawn let out for the day.

segments.speaker: Asia Mclean
segments.text: Adnan came in. He sat at the table. And we weren't really close friends or anything like that, but we knew each other. And we chatted or whatever. And I can't remember.

segments.speaker: Asia Mclean
segments.text: I think I must have asked him how he was doing or whatever, and he said fine. And he told me that him and Hae had broke up. And I was like, oh, well, that's a bummer. And I was like, what happened? And he was like, oh, well, she is seeing this other guy, some white dude.

segments.speaker: Asia Mclean
segments.text: But he was pretty chill about it. He was just like, you know, well, if she doesn't want to be with me, then that's fine. I just wish the best for her-- that kind of attitude.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I'm not sure why Asia's memory of this interaction is so clear all these years later. My best guess is that, because she wrote it down at the time in those letters and then the affidavit, that the details somehow stuck.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Do you remember what time you were talking, this would have happened in the library? Do you remember what time that conversation would have happened?

segments.speaker: Asia Mclean
segments.text: I don't. Because I know school let out around 2:15. So it was probably around 2:30.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
